Foreword The Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport) funded the National Laboratory of the Rockies to assess New England biomass feedstock availability and the potential to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in the region, along with an evaluation of jet fuel logistics. Key Takeaways • A resource assessment was conducted for ten New England Airports to quantify biomass feedstocks that could be used to produce biofuels including SAF. • Municipal solid waste, woody biomass, and food waste were found to be the most widely available resources. • The volume and type of biomass resources available near each airport vary significantly depending on the collection radius and local conditions such as population and land use. • A techno-economic analysis was conducted on total New England state (and select New York Counties) feedstocks to estimate a theoretical maximum total biofuel potential of 850 million gallons of gasoline equivalent per year.1,2 The purpose was to show that New England has sufficient feedstock to support SAF production facilities. • The analysis for bioenergy production potential for ten New England airports reveals strong opportunities for localized renewable fuel generation. • SAF produced outside of New England is expected to be pre-blended with Jet A in other markets such as New York Harbor and the Gulf Coast and delivered to New England via the same infrastructure that delivers Jet A today. • Enabling SAF produced in New England requires more consideration and planning due to infrastructure constraints. For example, the terminal supplying the highest volume of jet fuel can only receive fuel by barge or tanker, not by truck. • SAF produced in New England would be blended at a nearby terminal that can accommodate both blending and off-loading to a barge or tanker. • Many New England terminal owners expressed a willingness to work with future SAF producers to enable blending and delivery to airports within the region. Future regional SAF producers should work with the terminals identified in this report. 1 The theoretical maximum is based on all available feedstocks in the 6 New England states plus select New York counties (since the radii for multiple airports in this study draw from New York) would require multiple plant using different production technology pathways. 2 The proportion of SAF would depend on production technology pathways and biorefinery design.
